issues.legal_issue: Government land in a scheduled area cannot be leased or otherwise transferred to a non-tribal person for mining, subject to the exception for a State instrumentality or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.
material_facts: Mining leases for land in a notified scheduled area were granted by the State to non-tribal individuals and companies.
Some individual lessees transferred their mining interests to companies.
The lands included reserved forest and other land in the scheduled area.
issues.conclusion: The State is a person for purposes of the land-transfer restriction, and a lease transfers an interest in land. Government leases and transfers to non-tribals are void, except transfers to a State instrumentality or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.
issues.legal_principle: Article 244 and paragraph 5(2)(b) of the Fifth Schedule empower regulation of land allotment in scheduled areas for peace and good government; paragraph 5(2)(a) concerns restrictions on land transfers. Section 3(1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Area Land Transfer Regulation, as amended in 1970, prohibits transfers of immovable property in the scheduled area except to a Scheduled Tribe or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes. Article 298 is subject to the Constitution, including the Fifth Schedule. A lease is a transfer of an interest in land under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Court relied on P. Rami Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka, Lingappa Pochanna Appelwar v. State of Maharashtra, and M/s. Victoria Granites (P) Ltd. v. P. Rama Rao.

predicates.challenge_to_land_transfer_in_scheduled_: A proceeding challenged a land transfer or mining lease involving land in a scheduled area.
predicates.government_granted_mining_interest_to_no: The government granted or transferred a mining interest in the land to a person who was not a Scheduled Tribe member.
predicates.recipient_is_permitted_public_or_tribal_: The recipient was a State instrumentality or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a government mining grant in a scheduled area, a grant to a non-tribal recipient outside the stated public or tribal entities is void.

issues.legal_issue: Mining leases and renewals for non-forest purposes on forest land require prior approval from the Central Government.
material_facts: The mining leases covered land in reserved forests or other areas with forest character.
Mining was treated as a non-forest purpose.
The required prior approval had not been obtained for the impugned leases or renewals.
issues.conclusion: Mining leases and renewals for non-forest purposes on forest land without prior Central Government approval are invalid; the forest restriction is not confined to land formally declared a reserved forest.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires prior Central Government approval for, among other things, using forest land for a non-forest purpose or assigning forest land by lease to a private person. Forest land is not limited to land formally declared reserved forest. Mining is a non-forest purpose, and renewal also requires prior approval. The Court relied on Ambika Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Krishnadas Tikaram, and Tarun Bharat Sangh, Alwar v. Union of India; it held that State of Bihar v. Bansi Ram Modi no longer governed in light of the later decision in Ambika Quarry Works. The Court also referred to the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the environmental principles in Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India.

rule.if: challenge_to_forest_mining_lease and forest_land_used_for_nonforest_mining and not central_approval_obtained_before_use

predicates.challenge_to_forest_mining_lease: A proceeding challenged a mining lease or renewal involving forest land.
predicates.forest_land_used_for_nonforest_mining: Land with forest character was used for mining, which is a non-forest purpose.
predicates.central_approval_obtained_before_use: The Central Government granted approval before the forest land was used for the non-forest purpose.

issues.definition: A challenged mining lease or renewal using forest land for mining is invalid if prior Central Government approval was not obtained.

issues.legal_issue: Mining grants to non-tribals in scheduled areas are prohibited under the state-level restriction on mining leases, and renewal cannot avoid the prohibition.
material_facts: The mining areas were in scheduled areas inhabited by Scheduled Tribes.
The State-level mining restriction barred grants in those areas to persons who were not Scheduled Tribe members, subject to specified public or tribal exceptions.
Some leases had been transferred to non-tribal companies, and a renewal was sought or relied upon.
issues.conclusion: The State-level restriction prohibits grants to non-tribals in scheduled areas; a renewal is a fresh grant and cannot validate a prohibited non-tribal lease. Existing leases were independently held void under the land-transfer restriction and, where applicable, the forest law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(5) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, as amended by State law, prohibits mining leases in scheduled areas in favour of non-tribals, subject to the stated exception for a government-owned or controlled undertaking or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes. The Court treated the State amendment as prospective, while finding existing leases independently invalid under the Fifth Schedule, the Regulation, and the Forest (Conservation) Act. A renewal is in substance a fresh grant. The Court relied on M/s. Victoria Granites (P) Ltd. v. P. Rama Rao regarding transfers of mining leases.

predicates.challenge_to_scheduled_area_mining_grant: A proceeding challenged a mining grant or renewal in a scheduled area.
predicates.grant_or_renewal_for_nontribal_occurred_: The mining grant or renewal to a non-tribal occurred after a state-level restriction on such grants took effect.
predicates.recipient_is_permitted_public_or_tribal_: The recipient was a qualifying government-owned or controlled undertaking or a cooperative society composed solely of Scheduled Tribes.

issues.definition: A challenged post-restriction mining grant or renewal in a scheduled area is prohibited when it benefits a non-tribal recipient outside the stated public or tribal entities.

issues.legal_issue: Land cultivated and occupied by Scheduled Tribes within the identified enclosures is their patta land and cannot be leased by the government for mining.
material_facts: Scheduled Tribe families cultivated and occupied land within five identified enclosures.
A joint survey identified the enclosures as outside the reserved forest area.
The respondents conceded that the government had no power to grant mining leases over those lands.
issues.conclusion: The enclosure lands occupied and cultivated by the Scheduled Tribes are their patta lands, the concerned officers must grant the pattas, and the government cannot grant mining leases over them.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the protections for Scheduled Tribe land in the Fifth Schedule and the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Area Land Transfer Regulation, together with the factual finding that the enclosures had been excluded from the reserved forest area and were occupied and cultivated by the tribes. The judgment does not identify a separate earlier case as the basis for this specific determination.

predicates.challenge_to_mining_lease_over_tribal_en: A proceeding challenged a government mining lease over land in an enclosure occupied by Scheduled Tribes.
predicates.scheduled_tribes_occupy_and_cultivate_th: Scheduled Tribe families occupied and cultivated the land.
predicates.enclosure_is_outside_reserved_forest: The identified enclosure was outside the reserved forest area.

issues.definition: A government mining lease over an enclosure outside the reserved forest area is invalid when Scheduled Tribe families occupy and cultivate that land.

issues.legal_issue: An undertaking exploiting natural resources in a scheduled tribal area must protect the environment and provide for the social and economic welfare of the tribal community.
material_facts: The dispute concerned mining operations and mineral resources in a scheduled area inhabited by Scheduled Tribes.
The Court considered the effects of mining on tribal communities, forests, ecology, and access to basic services.
The Court directed that operators’ obligations include ecological protection and facilities such as water, education, health care, sanitation, transport, housing, and tribal employment.
issues.conclusion: Operators exploiting resources in scheduled areas must undertake and continuously discharge environmental and tribal-welfare obligations as part of their operations.
issues.legal_principle: The Court grounded these obligations in Articles 21, 39(b), and 46 of the Constitution, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It relied on the principles concerning life, livelihood, health, and environmental protection in Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India, Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India, Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India.

predicates.scheduled_area_resource_exploitation_dis: A proceeding concerned exploitation of natural resources in a scheduled area.
predicates.operator_exploits_natural_resources_in_t: An operator carried out or proposed to carry out resource exploitation in a tribal area.
predicates.tribal_community_is_affected: The resource exploitation affected the tribal community or its environment.

issues.definition: When resource exploitation in a scheduled tribal area affects the tribal community, the operator must fund tribal welfare and ecological protection.
